title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 28
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: Nitrogen Cycle and Agriculture
passages.text:
The nitrogen cycle is fundamental to all life on Earth, yet its management in agricultural systems remains one of the greatest challenges facing sustainable food production. Nitrogen, an essential macronutrient, is fixed from the atmosphere through biological and industrial processes, converted into forms usable by plants, and eventually returned to the atmosphere through bacterial decomposition and denitrification. This continuous cycle has operated for billions of years, but human agricultural practices have dramatically altered its pace and distribution.

In natural ecosystems, nitrogen cycles slowly through weathering of rocks, nitrogen fixation by free-living bacteria and legume-associated rhizobia, and denitrification by soil organisms. The process takes centuries or millennia to complete one full cycle. Industrial agriculture, however, has accelerated this timeline through synthetic fertilizer production, which consumes approximately 2 percent of global energy output annually. The Haber-Bosch process, developed in the early twentieth century, enabled the fixation of atmospheric nitrogen on an unprecedented industrial scale, allowing dramatic increases in crop yields. Today, synthetic nitrogen fertilizers support approximately half of the global population by enabling agricultural productivity sufficient to feed billions of people.

Yet this acceleration comes with significant environmental costs. Excess nitrogen from agricultural runoff accumulates in aquatic ecosystems, creating dead zones where oxygen depletion prevents most life from surviving. The Gulf of Mexico hypoxic zone, caused largely by runoff from Midwestern grain production in the United States, covers up to 8,500 square kilometres during summer months and has become a focal point for environmental concern. Nitrogen also enters groundwater supplies, contaminating drinking water and posing health risks to rural communities dependent on well water for their water supplies. Additionally, nitrogen fertilizer production generates substantial greenhouse gas emissions, particularly nitrous oxide, a potent climate forcing agent with a global warming potential nearly 300 times that of carbon dioxide over a century-long timeframe.

Agronomists and soil scientists are increasingly focused on nitrogen use efficiency — maximising crop productivity per unit of nitrogen applied to fields. Precision agriculture technologies, including variable-rate application systems and real-time soil sensors, allow farmers to match fertilizer application to plant demand more precisely than ever before possible. These systems reduce both environmental impacts and economic waste. Legume-based crop rotations, which restore soil nitrogen through symbiotic relationships with nitrogen-fixing bacteria, are experiencing renewed interest as farmers seek to reduce synthetic input costs and environmental impacts while maintaining productivity.

Balancing agricultural productivity with environmental stewardship requires integrated strategies combining precision management, crop diversity, and restoration of natural nitrogen cycling pathways. Without such comprehensive approaches, the benefits of the nitrogen-based green revolution risk being outweighed by accumulating environmental degradation in the coming decades.

passages.title: The Hubble Space Telescope
passages.text:
Launched on April 24, 1990, the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) has become humanity's most powerful tool for observing the distant universe and understanding cosmic phenomena. Positioned above Earth's atmosphere at an altitude of approximately 600 kilometres, Hubble avoids atmospheric distortion that limits ground-based telescopes, achieving a resolution roughly 100 times greater than Earth-bound observatories located on the surface. This remarkable capability has fundamentally transformed astronomical knowledge and popular understanding of the cosmos.

The telescope's early years were marked by technical disappointment and uncertainty. A flaw in the primary mirror's shape, discovered shortly after launch, severely degraded image quality until a repair mission in December 1993 installed corrective optics and restored functionality. This costly correction, along with subsequent maintenance missions by Space Shuttle astronauts, demonstrated the critical importance of human spaceflight capability and the value of serviceable space infrastructure. The repairs transformed Hubble from a flawed and expensive instrument into the revolutionary observatory it was originally intended to be, justifying the massive investment.

Hubble's scientific achievements fundamentally reshaped cosmology and our understanding of the universe. Observations of Cepheid variables — pulsating stars with well-understood brightness relationships — allowed astronomers to measure distances to nearby galaxies with unprecedented accuracy and confidence. These measurements revealed that the universe contains not just one galaxy, but billions, each containing billions of stars. In 1998, Hubble observations of distant supernovae provided evidence that cosmic expansion is accelerating, implying the existence of a mysterious dark energy component comprising approximately 70 percent of the universe's total mass and energy content. This discovery fundamentally altered our understanding of cosmic fate.

The telescope has also captured the public imagination through breathtaking images of nebulae, star-forming regions, and distant galaxies shown in vibrant detail. The Hubble Deep Field image, obtained in 1995 by pointing the telescope at a seemingly empty patch of sky roughly the size of a grain of sand held at arm's length, revealed thousands of galaxies in this infinitesimal region. Subsequent observations produced the Hubble Ultra Deep Field, containing approximately 10,000 visible galaxies in a space smaller than one ten-millionth of the entire sky.

Despite Hubble's advanced age — it is now over thirty years old and approaching the limits of its operational lifetime — the telescope continues producing discoveries. Recent observations have tracked the expansion history of the universe with improved precision, measured the properties of exoplanet atmospheres, and monitored dynamic changes in nearby galaxies. While the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, now provides complementary observations in the infrared spectrum, Hubble remains essential for visible-light and ultraviolet observations. As Hubble approaches the end of its operational lifetime, astronomers and the public alike reflect on its unparalleled contribution to human understanding of the universe.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is the primary role of nitrogen in biological systems?
questions.correctAnswer: It is an essential macronutrient required by all living organisms
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 identifies nitrogen as 'an essential macronutrient' required by organisms throughout its cycle.
options: It is an essential macronutrient required by all living organisms
It is released into the atmosphere only through decomposition
It serves only as an energy source for plants
It is produced exclusively by bacteria in the soil

questions.prompt: The word 'accelerated' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: increased in speed or rate
questions.explanation: 'Accelerated' means made faster; the passage indicates industrial agriculture has sped up nitrogen cycling compared to natural processes.
options: made more complex
increased in speed or rate
distributed unevenly
slowed down gradually

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what percentage of global energy is consumed by synthetic nitrogen fertilizer production?
questions.correctAnswer: Approximately 2 percent
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that synthetic nitrogen production 'consumes approximately 2 percent of global energy output annually.'
options: More than 10 percent
Less than 1 percent
Approximately 2 percent
About 5 percent

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the relationship between the Haber-Bosch process and global food security?
questions.correctAnswer: The process enabled dramatic increases in food production sufficient to support billions of people
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states the Haber-Bosch process 'enabled dramatic increases in crop yields' and that synthetic nitrogen 'supports approximately half of the global population.'
options: The process was abandoned due to environmental concerns
The process had minimal impact on agricultural productivity
The process made agriculture entirely dependent on fossil fuels
The process enabled dramatic increases in food production sufficient to support billions of people

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention the Gulf of Mexico hypoxic zone in paragraph 3?
questions.correctAnswer: To provide a specific example of dead zones caused by agricultural nitrogen runoff
questions.explanation: The author uses the Gulf of Mexico as a concrete example of how agricultural nitrogen causes hypoxic dead zones, demonstrating the environmental costs discussed.
options: To provide a specific example of dead zones caused by agricultural nitrogen runoff
To suggest that coastal fishing should be banned
To show that nitrogen runoff only affects saltwater ecosystems
To argue that all aquatic ecosystems are severely damaged

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a consequence of excess agricultural nitrogen?
questions.correctAnswer: Depletion of the ozone layer
questions.explanation: The passage mentions dead zones, groundwater contamination, and nitrous oxide emissions, but does not mention ozone depletion.
options: Emission of potent greenhouse gases
Depletion of the ozone layer
Dead zones in aquatic ecosystems
Contamination of drinking water supplies

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 4, what strategy involves restoring nitrogen to soil through natural biological processes?
questions.correctAnswer: Legume-based crop rotations utilizing nitrogen-fixing bacteria
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 identifies 'legume-based crop rotations, which restore soil nitrogen through symbiotic relationships with nitrogen-fixing bacteria' as a key strategy.
options: Increased application of synthetic fertilizers
Deep-water irrigation systems
Legume-based crop rotations utilizing nitrogen-fixing bacteria
Removal of all organic matter from soil

questions.prompt: The word 'precision' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: exactness and accuracy in measurement and application
questions.explanation: 'Precision agriculture' refers to applying inputs with high accuracy to match specific spatial and temporal needs.
options: cost-effectiveness
widespread geographical coverage
speed of implementation
exactness and accuracy in measurement and application

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in: 'Balancing agricultural productivity with environmental stewardship requires integrated strategies combining precision management, crop diversity, and restoration of natural nitrogen cycling pathways.'
questions.correctAnswer: Sustainable agriculture requires multiple coordinated approaches including technology, diversity, and natural processes
questions.explanation: The sentence identifies that solving the problem demands integration of several complementary strategies, not a single approach.
options: Sustainable agriculture requires multiple coordinated approaches including technology, diversity, and natural processes
The nitrogen cycle cannot be modified by human intervention
Agricultural productivity and environmental protection are mutually exclusive goals
Precision management alone is sufficient to solve nitrogen pollution

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.correctAnswer: B,D,E
questions.explanation: The three core ideas are: the industrial acceleration of nitrogen cycling (B), the major environmental consequences (D), and the need for integrated management strategies (E).
options: A. The Haber-Bosch process was invented in the late twentieth century and has had only minor impacts on agriculture.
B. Industrial agriculture has dramatically accelerated the nitrogen cycle through synthetic fertilizer production, supporting half the global population.
C. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria are found only in remote ecosystems and are irrelevant to modern agriculture.
D. Excess agricultural nitrogen creates dead zones, contaminates water supplies, and generates significant greenhouse gas emissions.
E. Sustainable solutions require balancing productivity with environmental protection through precision management, crop diversity, and restoration of natural cycling.
F. The nitrogen cycle operates identically in natural ecosystems and agricultural systems.

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in: 'While the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, now provides complementary observations in the infrared spectrum, Hubble remains essential for visible-light and ultraviolet observations.'
questions.correctAnswer: Although a newer telescope offers infrared data, Hubble is still necessary for visible and ultraviolet observations
questions.explanation: The sentence indicates both telescopes serve different but complementary functions, and Hubble remains valuable despite being older.
options: Hubble and James Webb observe the same spectrum of light
Although a newer telescope offers infrared data, Hubble is still necessary for visible and ultraviolet observations
Visible-light and ultraviolet observations have become unnecessary for modern astronomy
The James Webb Space Telescope has completely replaced Hubble for all observations

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.correctAnswer: A,C,E
questions.explanation: The passage's main themes are: Hubble's revolutionary observational capability and early technical challenges (A), its major scientific discoveries about the universe's composition and expansion (C), and its continued importance despite newer instruments (E).
options: A. The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990, faced early technical challenges, and has become one of astronomy's most powerful tools.
B. Hubble observations can only be conducted by Space Shuttle astronauts aboard the spacecraft.
C. Hubble observations have revealed the universe's vast scale, dark energy's existence, and the properties of distant galaxies.
D. The James Webb Space Telescope has completely replaced Hubble for all astronomical observations.
E. Despite being over thirty years old, Hubble continues producing discoveries and remains essential for visible and ultraviolet light observations.
F. The Hubble Deep Field image contained only a few hundred galaxies in a very small region of space.
